incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of AI-powered scammers who are using deepfake videos and fake social media profiles featuring his likeness to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals are offering fraudulent immigration services through hundreds of fake accounts, including promises of US residency for $2,200 and claims of help obtaining legal status. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began contacting his office about services he never provided. The situation has escalated dramatically over the past three months, with scammers directing victims through WhatsApp to send money via payment apps like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App.

An anti-piracy company hired by Leal's firm has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. The fraudulent videos also feature fake testimonials from supposed clients praising Leal's services. Leal is warning immigrants to verify identities of legal service providers and be suspicious of immediate payment requests, emphasizing that his office never requests payments over the phone. He plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the source of the scams.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article depicted Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated interview never occurred but was designed to promote an illegitimate investment scheme. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common as artificial intelligence makes it easier for criminals to create convincing fake content featuring well-known Australians.

ASIC reports that AI-generated investment scams are rising significantly, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake websites, news articles, reviews, and advertisements featuring impersonated celebrities and politicians. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated figure, followed by financial commentators like Alan Kohler, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers through official registers before investing, warning that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
Oura, a smart ring manufacturer valued at $11 billion, faces a class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco. The lawsuit alleges that Oura rings priced at $300 and up use misleading advertising about their sleep tracking capabilities. According to the suit, the company claims its devices can achieve 95 percent sleep staging accuracy comparable to clinical sleep labs, but the rings actually rely on artificial intelligence-generated guesses that are no more accurate than a coin flip. The lawsuit asserts that Oura's sensors and algorithms cannot detect the physiological signals necessary to accurately measure different sleep stages, since hospital labs require multiple electrodes to measure brain activity.

Oura responded by defending its science and research, stating that its rings estimate sleep stages using multiple physiological signals including heart rate, movement, and temperature, and that independent studies have validated its sleep staging against polysomnography. The company noted its product is not a medical device and should not replace clinical sleep studies. It remains unclear whether Oura Ring customers can join the suit or what compensation they might receive if the case proceeds to trial or settlement. This lawsuit follows another ongoing class-action suit against Oura alleging the company collected sensitive personal information without customer consent for two years.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team identified a ransomware group called Aurora that has been active since April 2026, targeting organizations worldwide. The group developed a Linux variant of their ransomware capable of attacking ESXi virtual machine environments. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to assist with hands-on exploitation across ten target organizations. The ransomware encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands, and the group operates a data leak site to publish stolen information.

Researchers discovered that Aurora uses a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to scan networks for VMware ESXi hypervisors and vCenter servers. A separate cluster of Aurora activity was also identified, affecting eight organizations across multiple countries including Israel, Germany, Spain, and the United States. This second group used different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The report provides technical indicators and command line options used by the ransomware, detailing how attackers systematically compromise and encrypt victim infrastructure.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee, Chaac Pizza Northeast, has filed a lawsuit claiming the chain's AI-powered delivery system caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut restaurants across New York, New Jersey, Maryland, Washington DC, and Pennsylvania. The company alleges that Pizza Hut forced adoption of Dragontail, a delivery management platform, which created operational problems and customer dissatisfaction. Before the system's rollout in 2024, Chaac maintained over 90 percent on-time deliveries within 30 minutes and achieved double-digit sales growth.

The lawsuit contends that Dragontail gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations, causing drivers to wait up to 15 minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than immediately delivering completed pizzas. Drivers could also see tip amounts and payment methods, making them less likely to accept certain orders. The franchisee claims this resulted in significant delivery delays, plummeting customer satisfaction, and sharp sales declines, with New York City locations experiencing a swing from 10.19 percent growth to 9.78 percent decline. Chaac accuses Pizza Hut of failing to provide adequate training or support and breaching the franchise agreement by mandating continued use of the problematic system.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A sophisticated scam has targeted authors, entertainers, and public figures by impersonating Terry Gross and the Fresh Air production team. Victims receive highly personalized emails that appear to offer interview opportunities on the popular radio show, complete with specific references to their work and professional booking details. Historian Jennifer Black from Misericordia University initially felt excited by such an invitation but became suspicious when the email seemed to come directly from Gross herself and included an artificial intelligence writing style. The scam escalates when recipients are asked to pay fees for production costs, with some victims also being directed to provide social media login credentials.

WHYY, NPR, and Fresh Air have confirmed they are investigating the fraudulent emails and have clarified that they never charge guests for interviews or offer payment. Cybersecurity expert Aunshul Rege explained that artificial intelligence has made it easier for scammers to create convincing, personalized impersonations of trusted figures. Red flags include requests for payment and emails from suspicious addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com. Rege recommends verifying interview invitations by contacting the organization directly through legitimate channels rather than responding to suspicious messages.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by Israel, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence systems. The institute, which has no legal entity status or physical address, presented pro-Israel arguments on contentious topics including allegations of genocide and war crimes in Gaza. The New York production company Piro Inc registered the site with the US Justice Department as material distributed for the Israeli government under foreign agent disclosure requirements. The reports were crafted to appear academically rigorous while consistently framing information to blunt criticism of Israel.

The campaign represents part of a broader effort funded by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government routed through the European advertising company Havas Media to manipulate chatbot responses. Contracts show the work involved deploying websites designed specifically to generate favorable results in AI conversations. The Hanover Institute's content has not been published since reports about it emerged in August 2026, though experts warn the material may already influence AI training data. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about such public diplomacy spending, noting that despite significant investment, American public opinion toward Israel has sharply declined since 2022.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and Capitol Records have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generation platforms. The labels accuse both companies of illegally scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and then directly reproducing sections of famous recordings in newly generated music. The record labels claim the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data, though both previously argued their use constitutes fair use. The lawsuits target the companies' headquarters in New York and Massachusetts respectively, and also name unnamed individuals allegedly involved in the scraping.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate versions of famous songs by using specific prompts that reference artists, decades, and musical styles. Examples include generating a song mimicking Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," a near-identical copy of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You," and a track that replicates Green Day's "American Idiot." The record labels submitted extensive documentation including a list of thousands of copyrighted works from artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, and Bruce Springsteen that they claim were used in training these AI models. The case raises significant questions about generative AI and copyright protection across music, art, video, and text.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers in a Los Angeles lawsuit admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in court filings. The case involves homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire left her Carson home uninhabitable. While repairs were underway, a storm caused additional water damage, and Meni-Siliga claims State Farm delayed approving repairs, ultimately leaving the work incomplete. She and her husband exhausted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure. State Farm initially blamed negligence by the plaintiff and others for her damages.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson, who prepared the filings for State Farm's law firm, acknowledged that seven case citations across eight motions did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. She mistakenly believed an artificial intelligence tool called Irys was linked to her legal research subscription and would verify citations. The discovery occurred in August when opposing counsel identified the errors during a court conference. The trial is scheduled for October, and the case highlights growing concerns about artificial intelligence use in law, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments now using generative AI.

stories.Headline: Electoral court sets new standards for AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Brazil's highest electoral court established new guidelines for identifying artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes in political content ahead of October elections. The ruling came from a case involving opposition candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who displayed AI-created images of his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, at his party's convention in July. The deepfake showed the former president endorsing his son's campaign against current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to lead a coup.

The court voted 4-3 to not punish Senator Bolsonaro, determining the deepfake was shown at a private party event rather than a public political advertisement. However, the court voted 5-2 to formally define what constitutes a deepfake in political advertising as synthetic content created or altered using artificial intelligence technology that realistically reproduces a person's image, voice, or speech. These standards will apply to thousands of campaign ads broadcasters must air before the October 4 election, during 14 minutes of daily airtime designated for political commercials.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $13 billion. Hugging Face is used by over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications on the platform. More than 200,000 companies also use the service. Nvidia's CEO stated that Hugging Face will remain an open-source platform, allowing organizations to download and customize their own AI models rather than paying for proprietary services from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The acquisition represents Nvidia's strategic bet that businesses will increasingly favor open-source AI models. This deal comes amid growing concerns about AI security, following several incidents where AI systems hacked into other organizations during testing. The $12.93 billion purchase includes $1 billion for employee retention. Nvidia's stock rose nearly 2% following the announcement, while Hugging Face remains privately held.

stories.Headline: NYC, the nation's largest school district, bans AI for students through 8th grade - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system announced a temporary one-year ban on artificial intelligence tools for students through eighth grade, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani described as the most expansive prohibition in the country. The policy prohibits all software using student-facing generative AI and bans companion chatbots across all grades. Meanwhile, the city will recommend screen time limits of 30 minutes daily for third through fifth graders and 45 minutes for sixth through eighth graders. Teachers remain allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

The broader approach aims to help students navigate AI while preventing over-reliance and cheating. High school students will receive AI literacy classes twice yearly and participate in supervised AI platform pilots. City officials will also conduct a comprehensive review of all technology tools in the school system and eliminate those deemed non-essential to learning. The teachers union praised the screen time limits but expressed concerns about implementation details and called for stronger safeguards in products the district purchases. Students are scheduled to return to classrooms the following week.

stories.Headline: Lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Yahoo
stories.Summary:
Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish basic standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence. Democratic state Senator Dina Neal recommended the committee pursue this action due to concerns about the lack of oversight and potential risks associated with integrating AI systems without legal requirements. The proposed legislation would require transparency around AI use and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems. Some people have reportedly been denied benefits and unable to speak with a human during appeals processes.

The nine bill draft requests, including the AI oversight proposal, were approved at an August 27 interim Government Affairs Committee meeting. The legislation will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. State Senator Edgar Flores emphasized the importance of ensuring humans ultimately make important decisions rather than relying solely on automated systems. Senator Neal said the state needs to audit agencies and determine how many errors have occurred where human response was needed but did not happen. Lawmakers anticipate facing resistance from state and local agencies when the bill is discussed.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.
